title: Nasseconset, Sachem of the Nissequogue
summary: Nasseconset was a Nissequogue sachem whose 1650 agreement and later challenge to Richard Smith preserve local landholding, payment disputes, and rights retained in the May 4, 1665 settlement.
content:
A sachem of the Nissequogue country

Nasseconset was a seventeenth-century sachem associated with the Nissequogue River country. Colonial records spell his name Nasseconseke, Nesatesconsett, and other ways. His documented activity extends from a 1650 land agreement to the disputes behind Smithtown’s settlement. Those records show a leader insisting that local ownership required recognition and payment.1

The river, neighboring meadows, and named necks of land organize his story. They were places with particular owners and uses, not an empty tract awaiting a town patent. His birth and death dates remain unknown.1

1650: a bargain with a payment deadline

An agreement printed at the beginning of the Smithtown records names Nasseconseke and English purchasers including members of the Wood family, Daniel Whitehead, and Stephen Hudson. Its bounds followed named rivers and necks, including Nesaquake and Conecticott.1

The promised payment included coats, wampum, hoes, hatchets, knives, kettles, and a hundred muxes, due by September 29, 1650. The document’s list of goods and deadline make the purchasers’ obligations visible alongside the land description.1

1664: challenging Richard Smith’s claim

Richard Smith later claimed land through Wyandanch’s 1659 gift to Lion Gardiner. In Smith’s own account, Nasseconset complained at the Setauket court in 1664 that Smith had taken his land. He distinguished the Cattawamnuck grant from land between the marked trees and the Nissequogue River that he maintained was his.1

Smith consulted Quashawam. According to his account, she acknowledged earlier transfers involving her father and brother but could not produce a written instrument. Smith then negotiated directly with Nasseconset. The sequence demonstrates that Gardiner’s deed had not settled every local claim.1

May 4, 1665: settlement and reserved interests

Smith’s account lists a gun, a kettle, ten coats, a blanket, and powder and lead as compensation. Catawump asserted an interest in half the land and received two additional coats. The settlement deed was dated May 4, 1665, following the complaint of the previous year.1

The deed’s Native marks include Nesatesconsett, Catawump, and Tanaringo. Its reservation names mats, canoes, eagles, and deer skins taken in the water. These retained interests sit within a document otherwise framed as a conveyance: ownership, access, and particular resources could remain separate questions.1

1666: family memory and overlapping rights

Testimony recorded on June 22, 1666 adds another perspective. Pauquatoun recalled that Wyandanch’s grandmother had lived on Cattawamnuck land. Quashawam explained that sachems connected by kinship to Tackapousha and to her parents had interests in the land and were to share payment.1

The testimony and Nasseconset’s complaint illuminate different parts of the same landscape. Together they reveal local proprietors, family connections, and compensation claims that a single founder’s deed cannot fully explain.1

References

Pelletreau, ed., Records of the Town of Smithtown (1898), pp. 1–2 (1650 Nasseconseke agreement), 3–5 (1659 family deed), 8–9 (1664 complaint and May 4, 1665 settlement), 16–17 (June 22, 1666 kinship testimony and October 18, 1667 boundary testimony).
why_this_matters: Nasseconset connects the Nissequogue River and Smithtown area to a named Indigenous leader, while reminding visitors that deeds preserve only a narrow colonial view of Native authority.
activity_update_summary: Expanded historical context, family and land connections, linked references, and dated Historic Moments.
